title: AP Statistics
description: Free AP Statistics study guide: 8 units, 320 practice questions, 80 flashcards, quick reference, memory tricks, and a full practice exam. Completely free.

units.name: Exploring Data

concepts.intro: Every distribution of quantitative data is described by its shape (symmetric, skewed, unimodal/bimodal), center (mean or median), and spread (range, IQR, or standard deviation), along with any outliers.
b: Always describe distributions with SOCS: Shape, Outliers, Center, Spread, in context
Skewed left: tail points left, mean < median; skewed right: tail points right, mean > median
Symmetric distributions have mean ≈ median
Unimodal = one peak, bimodal = two peaks, uniform = flat
Use the shape to decide which center/spread measures are appropriate

concepts.intro: The mean is the arithmetic average and is sensitive to outliers/skew, while the median is the middle value and resists extreme values.
b: Mean: x̄ = (Σx)/n
Median: middle value of ordered data (average of two middle values if n is even)
Mean is pulled toward the tail in a skewed distribution; median is resistant
For skewed data or data with outliers, report the median as the 'typical' value
Mode is the most frequent value; useful mainly for categorical or discrete data

concepts.intro: Spread describes how variable the data are; range and IQR are resistant-friendly, while variance and standard deviation use every value.
b: Range = max − min
IQR = Q3 − Q1 (spread of the middle 50%), resistant to outliers
Variance: s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1); Standard deviation s = √(variance)
SD measures the typical distance of a value from the mean
Standard deviation is not resistant — outliers inflate it
Use IQR with median (skewed data); use SD with mean (roughly symmetric data)

concepts.intro: The five-number summary (min, Q1, median, Q3, max) is displayed visually with a boxplot, and the 1.5×IQR rule flags potential outliers.
b: Five-number summary: Min, Q1, Median, Q3, Max
Outlier rule: any value below Q1 − 1.5(IQR) or above Q3 + 1.5(IQR)
Boxplots show the IQR as a box with whiskers to the most extreme non-outlier values
Modified boxplots plot outliers as separate points
Boxplots are good for comparing distributions across groups side by side

concepts.intro: A z-score converts a raw value into the number of standard deviations it lies from the mean, letting you compare values from different distributions.
b: z = (x − μ) / σ (or (x − x̄)/s for sample data)
Positive z: value is above the mean; negative z: value is below the mean
Standardizing does not change the shape of a distribution
z-scores allow comparison of values measured on different scales (e.g., test scores from different exams)
Adding a constant to every value shifts center but not spread; multiplying by a constant changes both center and spread proportionally

concepts.intro: When comparing two or more distributions, always compare shape, center, spread, and outliers in context rather than describing them separately.
b: Use parallel boxplots, back-to-back stemplots, or dotplots to compare groups
Comment on which group has the higher center and which has more/less variability
Relative frequency (percent) is used, not counts, when group sizes differ
Density curves show the proportion of data as area under the curve, total area = 1
Always write comparative statements in context, using words like 'greater than' or 'less variable than'

keyFacts: IQR = Q3 − Q1; outliers lie beyond Q1 − 1.5·IQR or Q3 + 1.5·IQR
z = (x − μ)/σ
Mean is pulled toward the tail in skewed data; median resists skew
traps: ‘Skewed left’ describes the direction of the longer tail, not where most data pile up
Standard deviation can never be negative; a computed negative SD means an arithmetic error
Adding a constant to all data shifts the mean but leaves the standard deviation unchanged — only multiplying changes spread
Comparing distributions requires comparative language in context, not two separate one-group descriptions

units.name: Modeling Distributions

concepts.intro: A density curve is a smooth curve that models the shape of a distribution, where the total area underneath equals 1 and area corresponds to proportion of data.
b: Total area under a density curve = 1 (100% of data)
Area under the curve over an interval = proportion of observations in that interval
The median divides the area in half; the mean is the balance point of the curve
In a skewed density curve, the mean is pulled toward the longer tail relative to the median
Density curves are idealized models, not the actual data

concepts.intro: The Normal distribution is a symmetric, bell-shaped density curve fully described by its mean μ and standard deviation σ, following the Empirical (68-95-99.7) Rule.
b: Notation: N(μ, σ)
68% of values fall within 1 SD of the mean (μ ± σ)
95% of values fall within 2 SD of the mean (μ ± 2σ)
99.7% of values fall within 3 SD of the mean (μ ± 3σ)
Normal curves are symmetric with mean = median = mode at the center
Inflection points of the curve occur at μ ± σ

concepts.intro: Any Normal distribution can be converted to the standard Normal distribution N(0,1) by standardizing values with z = (x − μ)/σ.
b: z = (x − μ)/σ converts x to a standard score
Standard Normal distribution: N(0, 1)
Use a z-table or calculator (normalcdf) to find proportions/probabilities
invNorm is used to find a value given a percentile/proportion
z-scores let you compare observations from different Normal distributions

concepts.intro: Calculator functions normalcdf and invNorm let you compute probabilities/proportions and find values from percentiles for any Normal distribution.
b: normalcdf(lower, upper, μ, σ) finds the proportion/probability between two values
invNorm(percentile, μ, σ) finds the value at a given percentile
For 'less than', use normalcdf(-1E99, x, μ, σ); for 'greater than', use normalcdf(x, 1E99, μ, σ)
Always sketch and shade the Normal curve before calculating
Check reasonableness: answers should be between 0 and 1 for probabilities

concepts.intro: A Normal probability plot (or comparing the data to the 68-95-99.7 rule) helps determine whether a data set is approximately Normally distributed.
b: A Normal probability plot that is roughly linear suggests the data are approximately Normal
Curvature in the plot indicates skewness or non-Normality
Compare observed percentages within 1, 2, 3 SD of the mean to 68%, 95%, 99.7%
Histograms/boxplots showing strong skew or outliers suggest data are not Normal
Many statistical procedures assume Normality, so checking it matters for inference later

keyFacts: Empirical Rule: 68% within ±1σ, 95% within ±2σ, 99.7% within ±3σ of μ
z = (x − μ)/σ ; x = μ + zσ
Total area under any density curve = 1
Standard Normal: N(0,1)
traps: The Empirical Rule only applies to (approximately) Normal distributions, not all distributions
A Normal probability plot with a clear curve — not a straight line — signals the data are NOT Normal
Area under a density curve represents proportion, not probability of a single exact point (P(X = x) = 0 for continuous variables)
z-scores can be negative; a negative z simply means the value is below the mean, not an error

units.name: Describing Bivariate Data

concepts.intro: A scatterplot displays the relationship between two quantitative variables, revealing direction, form, strength, and unusual features (outliers).
b: Explanatory variable (x) is plotted on the horizontal axis; response variable (y) on the vertical axis
Direction: positive (as x increases, y increases) or negative association
Form: linear or nonlinear (curved) pattern
Strength: how closely points follow the pattern (tight vs. scattered)
Always note any outliers or unusual points separately

concepts.intro: The correlation coefficient r measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two quantitative variables, ranging from -1 to 1.
b: r ranges from -1 to +1; sign matches the direction of association
r close to ±1 indicates a strong linear relationship; r close to 0 indicates a weak/no linear relationship
r measures only linear association — it can be misleading for curved relationships
r has no units and is not affected by which variable is x or y
r is strongly affected by outliers
r² (coefficient of determination) is discussed separately

concepts.intro: The least-squares regression line ŷ = a + bx minimizes the sum of squared residuals and is used to predict y from x.
b: Slope b = r(sy/sx); the line passes through (x̄, ȳ)
Interpretation of slope: 'for each one-unit increase in x, ŷ is predicted to change by b units'
Interpretation of y-intercept a: predicted value of y when x = 0 (only meaningful if x=0 is in scope)
Extrapolation (predicting far outside the observed x-range) is unreliable
Regression line is only appropriate for genuinely linear relationships

concepts.intro: A residual is the difference between an observed and predicted value (residual = y − ŷ), and residual plots help check whether a linear model is appropriate.
b: Residual = observed y − predicted ŷ
A residual plot with no pattern (random scatter around 0) supports a linear model
A curved pattern in the residual plot indicates the relationship is not linear
Increasing spread (fan shape) in residuals indicates non-constant variability
The sum of residuals for a least-squares line is always 0

concepts.intro: r² is the proportion of variation in y that is explained by the linear regression on x, and is always between 0 and 1.
b: r² = (correlation r)²
Interpretation: 'r²×100% of the variation in y is explained by the linear relationship with x'
r² closer to 1 means the regression line explains most of the variability in y
r² does not indicate causation, only explanatory strength of the linear model
Standard deviation of residuals (s) measures typical prediction error in y's units

concepts.intro: Outliers and especially influential points (often high-leverage x-values) can dramatically change the regression line, and nonlinear data may require transformation.
b: An outlier in regression has a large residual (far from the pattern)
An influential point substantially changes the slope/intercept if removed, often due to extreme x-value
Log or power transformations can linearize exponential or power-model data before regression
Always check a residual plot before trusting a linear model's predictions
Correlation/regression describe association, never prove causation

keyFacts: b = r(sy/sx); line passes through (x̄, ȳ)
r² = r²; proportion of variation in y explained by x
residual = y − ŷ; residuals sum to 0 for LSRL
-1 ≤ r ≤ 1; r measures strength/direction of LINEAR association only
traps: Correlation does NOT imply causation — a strong r only shows association
A high r² does not fix a nonlinear relationship; always check the residual plot first
Extrapolation beyond the observed x-range is unreliable even with a high r²
Correlation r is not resistant — a single outlier can drastically change its value

units.name: Designing Studies

concepts.intro: Good sampling methods use chance to select a subset of a population so the sample represents the whole population without bias.
b: Simple Random Sample (SRS): every group of n individuals has an equal chance of being chosen
Stratified random sample: population divided into homogeneous strata, then SRS taken within each stratum
Cluster sample: population divided into heterogeneous clusters, then entire clusters are randomly selected
Systematic sample: select every kth individual from a list after a random start
Convenience and voluntary response samples are NOT random and typically produce biased results

concepts.intro: Bias occurs when a sampling method systematically favors certain outcomes, making the sample not representative of the population.
b: Undercoverage: some groups of the population are left out of the sampling frame
Nonresponse bias: individuals selected don't respond, and responders differ from non-responders
Response bias: participants respond inaccurately due to question wording, interviewer, or social pressure
Voluntary response bias: sample consists only of people who choose to respond (e.g., call-in polls), often overrepresenting strong opinions
Larger sample size does NOT fix a biased sampling method

concepts.intro: An observational study measures variables without imposing treatments, while an experiment deliberately imposes treatments to study cause-and-effect.
b: Observational studies can show association but cannot establish causation due to potential confounding
Experiments impose a treatment on subjects and can establish causation if well-designed
Confounding variables are variables whose effects on the response cannot be separated from the explanatory variable's effect
Retrospective (case-control) and prospective (cohort) studies are types of observational studies
Random assignment (not random sampling) is what allows experiments to infer causation

concepts.intro: Well-designed experiments use control, randomization, and replication to reduce bias and allow cause-and-effect conclusions.
b: Control: control for lurking variables by comparing multiple treatments, e.g., including a control/placebo group
Randomize: use chance to assign subjects to treatment groups, balancing out lurking variables
Replicate: apply each treatment to many subjects to reduce the role of chance variation
Placebo effect: subjects respond simply to receiving any treatment; a placebo group controls for this
Double-blind: neither subjects nor those measuring the response know which treatment was given, reducing bias

concepts.intro: Blocking groups experimental units by a variable expected to affect the response before randomizing treatments within each block, increasing precision.
b: A block is a group of experimental units known to be similar in some way that affects the response (e.g., gender, age group)
Randomize treatments separately within each block ('block what you can, randomize what you cannot')
Matched pairs design: a special case of blocking with blocks of size two (e.g., before/after, or twins)
Blocking reduces variability from the blocking variable, making treatment effects easier to detect
Blocking is not the same as stratifying in sampling, though the logic is similar

concepts.intro: The scope of conclusions you can draw depends on whether random sampling and/or random assignment were used in a study.
b: Random sampling → results can be generalized to the population
Random assignment → cause-and-effect conclusions can be drawn
Random sampling AND random assignment → can generalize causal conclusions to the population
No randomization at all → conclusions apply only to the subjects studied, and only as association, not causation
Always identify explanatory and response variables, and check for confounding before making claims

keyFacts: SRS: every possible sample of size n is equally likely
Random assignment → causation; random sampling → generalizability
3 Principles of experimental design: Control, Randomize, Replicate
Block what you can, randomize what you cannot
traps: A large sample size cannot fix bias from a poor sampling method (e.g., a huge voluntary response sample is still biased)
Random sampling and random assignment are different: sampling allows generalization, assignment allows causal claims
Observational studies, no matter how large, cannot establish causation because of possible confounding variables
Blocking is done BEFORE random assignment; it's not the same as simply comparing groups after the fact

units.name: Probability & Simulation

concepts.intro: Probability quantifies the likelihood of an event, always between 0 and 1, and follows specific rules for combining events.
b: 0 ≤ P(A) ≤ 1 for any event A; P(sample space) = 1
Complement Rule: P(not A) = 1 − P(A)
Addition Rule (general): P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B)
Mutually exclusive (disjoint) events: P(A and B) = 0, so P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B)
Law of Large Numbers: as trials increase, the observed relative frequency approaches the true probability

concepts.intro: Two events are independent if the occurrence of one does not change the probability of the other; this is a different concept from mutually exclusive events.
b: Events A and B are independent if P(A|B) = P(A) (and equivalently P(B|A) = P(B))
Mutually exclusive events CANNOT both occur (P(A and B) = 0); independent events CAN both occur
Mutually exclusive events with nonzero probabilities are NEVER independent
Check independence with the multiplication rule: P(A and B) = P(A)×P(B) only if independent
Real-world context often needs the general multiplication rule if events aren't independent

concepts.intro: Conditional probability P(A|B) gives the probability of event A occurring given that event B has already occurred, restricting the sample space to B.
b: P(A|B) = P(A and B) / P(B), provided P(B) > 0
Two-way tables are useful for computing conditional probabilities directly from counts
Conditional probability restricts attention to only the outcomes where the given condition is true
Order matters: P(A|B) is generally not equal to P(B|A)
Use conditional probability to formally test for independence

concepts.intro: The multiplication rule finds the probability that two events both occur: P(A and B) = P(A)×P(B|A), simplifying to P(A)×P(B) when independent.
b: General rule: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B|A)
If A and B are independent: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)
Tree diagrams visually organize sequential/conditional probabilities and multiply along branches
Sampling without replacement typically creates dependent events (probabilities change after each draw)
Sampling with replacement typically creates independent events

concepts.intro: Simulation uses random number generators (or physical devices) to imitate chance behavior, estimating probabilities that are hard to calculate directly.
b: Steps: (1) State the assumptions/model, (2) Assign digits/outcomes to represent events, (3) Run many trials, (4) Compute the estimated probability from the results
More trials produce a more accurate simulation estimate (Law of Large Numbers)
Simulation gives an APPROXIMATION of the true probability, not an exact answer
Random digit tables or calculator random number generators (randInt) are common tools
Clearly define what constitutes 'success' in each trial before running the simulation

concepts.intro: Two-way tables organize data by two categorical variables, and Venn diagrams visually represent unions, intersections, and complements of events.
b: Marginal probability: probability based on a row or column total divided by the grand total
Joint probability: probability of the intersection of two specific categories (a single cell / grand total)
Venn diagram overlap represents 'and' (intersection); combined regions represent 'or' (union)
Two-way tables make it easy to compute conditional probabilities: (cell count)/(row or column total)
Check independence in a two-way table by comparing conditional and marginal probabilities

keyFacts: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B); if disjoint, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B)
P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B)
P(A and B) = P(A)×P(B|A); if independent, = P(A)×P(B)
Independent ≠ Mutually Exclusive: disjoint events with P>0 are never independent
traps: Mutually exclusive events are NOT independent (if both have positive probability) — a very common mix-up
P(A|B) ≠ P(B|A) in general — order and conditioning direction matter
'At least one' problems are usually easiest using the complement rule: P(at least one) = 1 − P(none)

Sampling without replacement changes probabilities from draw to draw, creating dependence, even if it 'feels' independent for large populations (approximately independent only when population is much larger than sample)

units.name: Random Variables

concepts.intro: A discrete random variable X takes a countable set of numeric values, each with a probability; the probability distribution lists every value with P(X = x).
b: Valid distribution requires every P(x) ≥ 0 and ΣP(x) = 1
Probability histograms display the distribution visually; shape, center, and spread all matter
P(X = a) is a single bar; P(X ≤ a) or P(X ≥ a) sums the relevant bars (cumulative probability)
Discrete RVs take isolated values (counts); continuous RVs take any value in an interval (measured with density curves/area)
Use two-way tables or context to build a distribution from raw counts before computing summary values

concepts.l: Expected Value (Mean) of a Random Variable
concepts.intro: The expected value μX is the long-run average outcome of a random variable if the chance process were repeated infinitely many times — a probability-weighted average, not a typical single outcome.
b: μX = E(X) = Σ x·P(x), summing over every possible value
E(X) need not be a value X can actually take (e.g., average number of children = 2.3)
For a linear transformation: E(a + bX) = a + b·E(X)
For the sum of two random variables: E(X + Y) = E(X) + E(Y), always — no independence needed
E(X − Y) = E(X) − E(Y), always true as well

concepts.l: Variance and Standard Deviation of a Random Variable
concepts.intro: Variance measures the average squared deviation of a random variable from its mean, quantifying spread; standard deviation is its square root, back in the original units.
b: σ²X = Var(X) = Σ (x − μX)²·P(x); σX = √ Var(X)
For a linear transformation: Var(a + bX) = b²·Var(X); adding a constant a never changes spread
If X and Y are INDEPENDENT: Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) and Var(X − Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) — variances always add for independent RVs, even when subtracting
Standard deviations do NOT add or subtract directly; you must add variances first, then take the square root
Combining random variables that are NOT independent requires a covariance term, which is beyond the standard AP formula but the AP exam assumes independence unless stated otherwise

concepts.intro: New random variables formed by adding, subtracting, or scaling other random variables follow predictable rules for their mean and variance.
b: Mean of a sum/difference: μ(X±Y) = μX ± μY, regardless of independence
Variance of a sum/difference (independent X, Y only): σ²(X±Y) = σ²X + σ²Y
Example: total time for two independent tasks — add means and add variances, then take the square root for the combined SD
Watch units and context carefully: 'X − Y' models a difference in outcomes, not a probability of X being less than Y
Check independence explicitly before adding variances; dependent variables need extra (non-AP-formula) covariance information

concepts.intro: A binomial random variable counts the number of successes in a fixed number of independent trials, each with the same two possible outcomes and the same probability of success.
b: BINS conditions: Binary outcomes, Independent trials, fixed Number of trials n, Same probability p of success on each trial
P(X = k) = C(n,k)·p^k·(1−p)^(n−k), where C(n,k) = n!/(k!(n−k)!)
Mean: μX = np; Standard deviation: σX = √(np(1−p))
10% condition: sampling without replacement from a finite population is approximately independent (binomial-like) only if the sample is less than 10% of the population
Large Counts condition (np ≥ 10 and n(1−p) ≥ 10) allows a Normal approximation to the binomial distribution

concepts.intro: A geometric random variable counts the number of trials needed to get the FIRST success in a sequence of independent trials with constant probability of success.
b: Conditions are BITS: Binary outcomes, Independent trials, constant probability p, trials continue until the first Success (no fixed n)
P(X = k) = (1−p)^(k−1)·p, for k = 1, 2, 3, … (X starts at 1, not 0)
Mean: μX = 1/p; Standard deviation: σX = √((1−p)/p²)
P(X > n) = (1−p)^n, the probability of no success in the first n trials
Distinguish from binomial: geometric has no fixed number of trials and asks 'how long until,' while binomial fixes n and counts successes

keyFacts: E(X) = Σ x·P(x); Var(X) = Σ (x−μ)²·P(x); σX = √Var(X)
Linear transform: E(a+bX) = a+b·E(X); Var(a+bX) = b²·Var(X)
Binomial: μ = np, σ = √(np(1−p)); P(X=k) = C(n,k)p^k(1−p)^(n−k)
Geometric: μ = 1/p, σ = √((1−p)/p²); P(X=k) = (1−p)^(k−1)p
traps: Variances add for independent RVs even when you SUBTRACT the variables: Var(X−Y) = Var(X)+Var(Y), not Var(X)−Var(Y)
Standard deviations never add or subtract directly — always combine variances first, then take the square root at the end
A binomial variable requires a FIXED number of trials n; if the question asks 'how many trials until the first success,' that's geometric, not binomial
Geometric random variables start at X = 1 (you need at least one trial), never at X = 0

units.name: Sampling Distributions

concepts.intro: A sampling distribution describes the distribution of a statistic (like a sample mean or sample proportion) computed from every possible sample of a given size — it tells us how much a statistic varies from sample to sample.
b: A statistic (from a sample) estimates a parameter (from the population); statistics vary, parameters are fixed
The sampling distribution's shape, center, and spread describe how the statistic behaves across repeated sampling
An estimator is unbiased if the mean of its sampling distribution equals the true parameter value
Variability of a sampling distribution decreases as sample size n increases
Bias relates to accuracy (centered on the parameter); variability relates to precision (how spread out the statistic's values are)

concepts.l: Sampling Distribution of a Sample Proportion
concepts.intro: When repeatedly sampling from a population with true proportion p, the sample proportion p̂ has a predictable mean, standard deviation, and (under conditions) approximately Normal shape.
b: Mean: μp̂ = p (p̂ is an unbiased estimator of p)
Standard deviation: σp̂ = √(p(1−p)/n)
10% condition: sample size n must be less than 10% of the population for independence (so σp̂ formula is accurate)
Large Counts condition: np ≥ 10 and n(1−p) ≥ 10 for the sampling distribution of p̂ to be approximately Normal
As n increases, σp̂ decreases (more precise estimates), but the mean stays at p

concepts.l: Sampling Distribution of a Sample Mean
concepts.intro: When repeatedly sampling from a population with mean μ and standard deviation σ, the sample mean x̄ has its own sampling distribution with predictable mean and standard deviation.
b: Mean: μx̄ = μ (x̄ is an unbiased estimator of μ) — true for any sample size
Standard deviation (standard error): σx̄ = σ/√n, requires the 10% condition when sampling without replacement
If the population itself is Normally distributed, x̄ is exactly Normally distributed for any n
If the population is NOT Normal, x̄'s distribution becomes approximately Normal as n grows large (Central Limit Theorem)
Increasing n reduces σx̄ (more precision) but does not change μx̄

concepts.intro: The Central Limit Theorem states that as sample size n increases, the sampling distribution of the sample mean x̄ approaches a Normal distribution, regardless of the shape of the population distribution.
b: Rule of thumb: CLT applies well once n ≥ 30 for most population shapes, though strongly skewed populations may need larger n
CLT justifies using Normal-based procedures (z-scores, confidence intervals) for means even when the population isn't Normal
The CLT applies to sums and means of independent, identically distributed random variables
The CLT does NOT change μx̄ = μ or σx̄ = σ/√n — it only affects the SHAPE of the sampling distribution
For proportions, the analogous Large Counts condition (np≥10, n(1−p)≥10) plays a similar Normal-approximation role

concepts.l: Standard Error and the Effect of Sample Size
concepts.intro: Standard error is the estimated standard deviation of a sampling distribution when the population parameter is unknown; it shrinks as sample size grows, following an inverse square-root relationship.
b: Standard error of p̂: SE(p̂) = √(p̂(1−p̂)/n), using the sample proportion since p is unknown
Standard error of x̄: SE(x̄) = s/√n, using the sample standard deviation s since σ is unknown
To cut the standard error in half, you must QUADRUPLE the sample size (since σ/√n involves a square root)
Larger samples give more precise (less variable) estimates, but do not remove bias caused by poor sampling methods
Larger sample size never fixes a biased sampling method — that requires proper random sampling design, not more data

keyFacts: μx̄ = μ; σx̄ = σ/√n
CLT: shape of x̄'s sampling distribution → approximately Normal as n grows (rule of thumb n≥30)
Large Counts (proportions): np≥10 and n(1−p)≥10; 10% condition needed for independence in both cases
traps: Increasing sample size reduces variability (σ/√n) but never removes bias from a flawed sampling method
σx̄ = σ/√n, NOT σ/n — a common algebra slip that badly underestimates spread
The CLT describes the SHAPE of the sampling distribution of x̄, not the shape of the original population data
To halve the standard error, you must quadruple n, not just double it, because of the square root in σ/√n

units.name: Inference: Confidence & Tests

concepts.intro: A confidence interval uses a sample statistic plus a margin of error to estimate an unknown population parameter, with a stated level of confidence in the method used to produce it.
b: General form: statistic ± (critical value)×(standard error)
Confidence level describes the long-run capture rate of the METHOD: e.g., 95% of all intervals built this way would capture the true parameter over many repetitions
Higher confidence level → wider interval (larger critical value), all else equal
Larger sample size → narrower interval (smaller standard error), all else equal
Conditions to check: Random (random sample/assignment), Normal/Large Counts (shape of sampling distribution), Independent (10% condition)

concepts.l: Confidence Interval for a Proportion and a Mean
concepts.intro: The one-proportion z-interval and one-sample t-interval are the two core confidence interval procedures for estimating a population proportion or population mean.
b: One-proportion z-interval: p̂ ± z*·√(p̂(1−p̂)/n)
One-sample t-interval for a mean: x̄ ± t*·(s/√n), using t* from a t-distribution with n−1 degrees of freedom because σ is unknown
The t-distribution is shorter and wider (fatter tails) than the Normal distribution, especially for small n, to account for extra uncertainty from estimating σ with s
As degrees of freedom (n−1) increase, the t-distribution approaches the standard Normal distribution
Common critical values: z*=1.645 (90%), 1.96 (95%), 2.576 (99%); t* depends on both confidence level and df (found via table or technology)

concepts.intro: A hypothesis test uses sample evidence to assess a claim about a population, weighing the null hypothesis (no effect/no difference) against an alternative hypothesis.
b: H0 (null): typically states 'no effect' or equality (e.g., p = 0.5, μ1 = μ2); Ha (alternative): what we suspect is true (≠, <, or >)
The P-value is the probability of getting a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed, ASSUMING H0 is true
Small P-value = strong evidence against H0; if P-value < α (significance level), reject H0; otherwise, fail to reject H0
'Fail to reject H0' is NOT the same as 'accept H0' or 'prove H0 true' — it just means insufficient evidence against it
Same Random/Normal(or Large Counts)/Independent conditions from confidence intervals also apply before running a hypothesis test

concepts.l: Type I and Type II Errors, and Power
concepts.intro: Every hypothesis test risks two types of mistakes: rejecting a true null hypothesis (Type I) or failing to reject a false null hypothesis (Type II); power measures the test's ability to correctly detect a real effect.
b: Type I error: rejecting H0 when H0 is actually TRUE; P(Type I error) = α, the significance level
Type II error: failing to reject H0 when H0 is actually FALSE (Ha is true); P(Type II error) = β
Power = 1 − β = the probability of correctly rejecting a false H0; higher power is better
Decreasing α (e.g., from 0.05 to 0.01) reduces the risk of Type I error but INCREASES the risk of Type II error (lowers power)
Increasing sample size increases power without increasing α, because it reduces standard error

concepts.l: t-Tests, Chi-Square Tests, and Choosing a Procedure
concepts.intro: Different inference procedures fit different data types: t-tests compare means, chi-square tests analyze categorical count data, and each has its own test statistic and distribution.
b: One-sample t-test statistic: t = (x̄ − μ0)/(s/√n), with df = n−1
Two-sample t-test statistic (independent samples): t = (x̄1 − x̄2)/√(s1²/n1 + s2²/n2), for comparing two population means
Chi-square test statistic: χ² = Σ (observed − expected)²/expected, used for goodness-of-fit, homogeneity, or independence tests with categorical data
Chi-square goodness-of-fit compares one categorical variable to a hypothesized distribution; chi-square test for independence/association examines two categorical variables in a two-way table
Choose a proportion procedure (z) for categorical data summarized as counts/percentages; choose a t-procedure for quantitative data summarized as means

keyFacts: CI form: statistic ± (critical value)×(SE); proportion: p̂ ± z*√(p̂(1−p̂)/n); mean: x̄ ± t*(s/√n), df=n−1
Test statistic: (statistic − hypothesized value)/(standard error); one-sample t: (x̄−μ0)/(s/√n)
χ² = Σ(observed−expected)²/expected
P(Type I error)=α; P(Type II error)=β; Power=1−β
traps: 'Fail to reject H0' does NOT mean H0 is proven true — it only means there's insufficient evidence against it
A P-value is NOT the probability that H0 is true; it's the probability of data this extreme (or more) GIVEN H0 is true
Decreasing α to reduce Type I error risk INCREASES the risk of Type II error (lowers power) — you can't minimize both simultaneously without changing the sample size
Confidence level describes the long-run success rate of the METHOD across many samples, not the probability that one specific interval contains the true parameter

quiz.q: A distribution has mean 50 and median 60 with a long tail to the left. This distribution is best described as:
quiz.e: Mean less than median with a long left tail indicates left skew.

quiz.q: Which measure of center is resistant to outliers?
quiz.e: The median only depends on the middle value(s), so extreme values don't affect it much.

quiz.q: A data set: 2, 4, 4, 6, 9. Find the mean.
For the data set 2, 4, 4, 6, 9, what is the median?
quiz.e: Ordered data's middle value (3rd of 5) is 4.

quiz.q: If a distribution is strongly skewed right, which measure of center is more appropriate to report?
quiz.e: Median resists the pull of the long right tail and reflects the typical value.

quiz.q: The IQR of a data set is the difference between:
quiz.e: IQR = Q3 − Q1, the spread of the middle 50% of data.

quiz.q: A value is an outlier by the 1.5×IQR rule if it is:
quiz.e: The 1.5×IQR rule flags values more than 1.5 IQRs below Q1 or above Q3.

quiz.q: Data set has Q1 = 10, Q3 = 22. What is the upper fence for outliers?
Which of the following is NOT resistant to outliers?
quiz.e: Standard deviation uses every value including extreme ones, so it is not resistant.

quiz.q: A test score of 82 has a z-score of 1.5 when μ = 70 and σ = 8. Is this consistent?
quiz.e: (82-70)/8 = 12/8 = 1.5, so the z-score is correct.

quiz.q: A z-score tells you:
o: How many standard deviations a value is from the mean
quiz.e: z-scores measure distance from the mean in standard deviation units.

quiz.q: If every value in a data set is multiplied by 3, what happens to the standard deviation?
quiz.e: Multiplying data by a constant multiplies the SD by the absolute value of that constant.

quiz.q: If a constant of 5 is added to every data value, the standard deviation:
quiz.e: Adding a constant shifts every value equally, changing the mean/median but not the spread.

quiz.q: A boxplot's box represents:
quiz.e: The box spans from Q1 to Q3, capturing the middle 50% of the data.

quiz.q: In a boxplot, whiskers extend to:
o: The most extreme values that are not outliers
Exactly 1.5 IQR from the box always
quiz.e: Whiskers reach the most extreme data points within the fences (non-outliers).

quiz.q: When comparing two groups' distributions, you should:
o: Describe each group separately with no comparison
Use comparative language like 'greater than' in context
quiz.e: AP scoring requires explicit comparative statements in context, e.g., 'Group A has a higher median than Group B.'

quiz.q: A distribution is symmetric and unimodal. Which relationship best fits?
quiz.e: In symmetric distributions, mean and median are approximately equal.

quiz.q: Which plot is best for comparing the shapes of two large data sets side-by-side?
quiz.e: Parallel boxplots or back-to-back stemplots allow visual comparison of shape, center, and spread.

quiz.q: The variance is defined as:
quiz.e: Sample variance s² = Σ(x−x̄)²/(n−1).

quiz.q: Standard deviation is the square root of:
quiz.e: By definition, s = √(s²), the square root of variance.

quiz.q: A data set has an SD of 0. What does this tell you?
quiz.e: SD = 0 only if there is no variability, meaning every value equals the mean.

quiz.q: Which of the following would most increase the standard deviation of a data set?
o: Adding a value far from the mean
Adding a value equal to the mean
quiz.e: Adding a value far from the mean increases the squared deviations, raising SD.

quiz.q: For a right-skewed distribution, which is typically true?
quiz.e: In right skew, the long right tail pulls the mean above the median.

quiz.q: A frequency table shows 10 students scored 60-69, 15 scored 70-79, 5 scored 80-89. This is an example of:
quiz.e: Grouping values into intervals with counts is grouped/binned frequency data.

quiz.q: Which statistic uses only two of the five-number summary values?
quiz.e: IQR = Q3 − Q1, using only two of the five-number summary's values.

quiz.q: A percentile of 90 means:
o: 90% of values are above this value
90% of values are at or below this value
The value is 90 units above the mean
quiz.e: The pth percentile is the value below which p% of the data fall.

quiz.q: Which is more affected by an extreme outlier: mean or median?
quiz.e: The mean incorporates every value directly into its sum, so a single extreme value shifts it substantially.

quiz.q: A cumulative relative frequency graph (ogive) is used to find:
quiz.e: Ogives plot cumulative percentages, letting you read off percentiles and the median.

quiz.q: If a distribution is uniform, its shape is:
o: Flat, roughly equal frequency across values
quiz.e: Uniform distributions have roughly constant frequency/density across the range.

quiz.q: A stemplot splitting stems by 'leaves 0-4' and 'leaves 5-9' is called:
quiz.e: A split stemplot divides each stem into two lines to show more detail in the shape.

quiz.q: A set of data has mean 20 and SD 4. Convert x = 28 to a z-score.
With mean 100 and SD 15 (like IQ scores), what raw score corresponds to z = -1?
Which graphical display is most appropriate for a single quantitative variable's shape?
quiz.e: Histograms display the distribution shape of quantitative data using bins.

quiz.q: A pie chart is appropriate for:
o: Categorical data showing parts of a whole
quiz.e: Pie charts represent proportions of categories, not quantitative distributions.

quiz.q: Which is true about the sum of deviations from the mean, Σ(x − x̄)?
quiz.e: By definition, deviations from the mean sum to zero, which is why squared deviations are used for variance.

quiz.q: A class's exam scores are heavily skewed left with several low outliers. The best summary uses:
quiz.e: Median and IQR are resistant to skew and outliers, making them appropriate here.

quiz.q: Which change to a data set would NOT affect the IQR?
o: Adding a constant to every value
Multiplying every value by a constant
quiz.e: Adding a constant shifts all values equally, so Q3 − Q1 (IQR) is unchanged.

quiz.q: Two data sets have the same mean but different standard deviations. What does the larger SD indicate?
quiz.e: A larger SD indicates data points are more spread out from the mean on average.

quiz.q: A z-score of -2.5 for a value means:
o: The value is 2.5 units above the mean
The value is 2.5 standard deviations below the mean
quiz.e: Negative z-scores indicate the value lies below the mean, here by 2.5 SDs.

quiz.q: When describing shape, 'bimodal' means the distribution has:
quiz.e: Bimodal distributions show two distinct peaks, often suggesting two underlying groups.

quiz.q: A Normal distribution has μ = 100, σ = 15. What percent of values fall between 85 and 115?
quiz.e: 85 and 115 are μ ± 1σ, capturing 68% by the Empirical Rule.

quiz.q: For N(100, 15), what range captures 95% of values?
quiz.e: 95% falls within μ ± 2σ = 100 ± 30, i.e., 70 to 130.

quiz.q: What is the z-score for x = 130 in N(100, 15)?
In a standard Normal distribution, what is P(Z < 0)?
quiz.e: The standard Normal is symmetric about 0, so exactly half the area lies below 0.

quiz.q: Total area under any density curve equals:
quiz.e: By definition, the total area under a density curve is always 1 (100%).

quiz.q: Which best describes the Normal distribution's shape?
quiz.e: The Normal distribution is symmetric and bell-shaped, centered at μ.

quiz.q: For N(50, 10), what is the value at the 84th percentile (approximately)?
quiz.e: 84th percentile ≈ μ + 1σ (since 50% + 34% ≈ 84%), so 50+10 = 60.

quiz.q: A student scores z = -1.5 on an exam that is N(75, 8). What is their raw score?
Which calculator function finds the proportion of area between two z-values?
quiz.e: normalcdf(lower, upper, μ, σ) computes the area (proportion) between two values.

quiz.q: Which calculator function finds a value given a percentile?
quiz.e: invNorm(area, μ, σ) returns the x-value corresponding to a given cumulative proportion.

quiz.q: A Normal probability plot that curves noticeably suggests:
o: The sample size is too large
quiz.e: Systematic curvature in a Normal probability plot indicates departure from Normality.

quiz.q: What proportion of a Normal distribution lies more than 2 SD from the mean?
quiz.e: Since 95% lies within 2 SD, the remaining 5% lies beyond ±2σ (both tails combined).

quiz.q: For a standard Normal variable, P(Z > 1.96) is approximately:
quiz.e: About 2.5% of the area lies in each tail beyond ±1.96 in the standard Normal (from the 95% rule).

quiz.q: A data set's middle 68% closely matches ±1 SD from the mean, and a Normal probability plot is roughly linear. This suggests:
quiz.e: Both pieces of evidence — matching Empirical Rule percentages and a linear probability plot — support approximate Normality.

quiz.q: If X ~ N(20, 5), what is P(X < 20)?
quiz.e: 20 is the mean, and Normal distributions are symmetric, so exactly half the area lies below the mean.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a property of the Normal distribution?
quiz.e: The Normal distribution extends from -∞ to +∞; it is not bounded between 0 and 1 (that describes probability values, not x-values).

quiz.q: For N(0,1), invNorm(0.5) equals:
quiz.e: The median (50th percentile) of the standard Normal distribution is 0.

quiz.q: A z-score of 0 means the value is:
quiz.e: z = 0 occurs only when x = μ, since z = (x−μ)/σ.

quiz.q: Which is the correct way to compute P(X > 85) for N(80, 6)?
quiz.e: 'Greater than 85' uses the upper tail: normalcdf from 85 to infinity.

quiz.q: A distribution's Normal probability plot is a straight, roughly 45° line. This indicates:
o: Good fit to a Normal model
quiz.e: A linear Normal probability plot indicates the data closely follow a Normal distribution.

quiz.q: What is the interquartile range of the standard Normal distribution, approximately?
quiz.e: Q1 ≈ -0.675 and Q3 ≈ 0.675 for N(0,1), giving IQR ≈ 1.35.

quiz.q: Heights of adult men are approximately N(70, 3) inches. What percent are taller than 76 inches?
quiz.e: 76 is 2 SD above the mean (70+2×3); about 2.5% of a Normal distribution lies beyond +2σ in one tail.

quiz.q: Which value is closer to the mean in a right-skewed distribution: the mean or the median?
quiz.e: In skewed distributions, the median is less affected by the tail and stays closer to the bulk of the data than the mean.

quiz.q: For X ~ N(60, 8), find the z-score for x = 44.
Approximately what percent of a Normal distribution lies between the mean and 1 SD above it?
quiz.e: Half of the 68% within ±1σ lies on each side, so about 34% lies between the mean and +1σ.

quiz.q: A calculator gives invNorm(0.90, 100, 15) = 119.2. This means:
quiz.e: invNorm returns the value below which the given proportion (90%) of the distribution lies.

quiz.q: Which scenario is LEAST likely to be well-modeled by a Normal distribution?
o: Measurement errors in a precise instrument
quiz.e: Income distributions are typically strongly right-skewed, not Normal.

quiz.q: If a distribution is exactly Normal, what is true of skewness?
quiz.e: Normal distributions are perfectly symmetric, so skewness is zero.

quiz.q: The 'inflection points' of a Normal curve occur at:
quiz.e: The curve changes concavity (inflection) exactly one standard deviation from the mean on each side.

quiz.q: A test is Normally distributed with mean 500 and SD 100. What score is at the 97.5th percentile (approx)?
quiz.e: 97.5th percentile ≈ μ + 2σ (since 95% is within ±2σ, leaving 2.5% above), so 500+200 = 700.

quiz.q: Which is true about comparing z-scores from two different Normal distributions?
o: A higher z-score always means a higher raw score in both distributions and standardized comparisons are valid
Only means can be compared, not z-scores
quiz.e: Standardizing puts values on a common scale, so z-scores can be validly compared across different Normal distributions.

quiz.q: Which best describes 'proportion of area under a density curve between a and b'?
o: The count of values between a and b
The proportion of observations between a and b
The mean of values between a and b
The SD between a and b
quiz.e: Area under a density curve directly represents the proportion of the distribution in that interval.

quiz.q: For a Normal distribution, which measure of center and spread fully determine the curve?
quiz.e: A Normal distribution N(μ, σ) is completely specified by its mean and standard deviation.

quiz.q: What is P(Z < -1.5) for the standard Normal distribution, approximately?
quiz.e: Using the standard Normal table, P(Z < -1.5) ≈ 0.0668, closest to 0.07.

quiz.q: Test scores are N(70, 10). A score of 90 is how many standard deviations above the mean?
Which statement about the median of a Normal distribution is true?
o: It is always less than the mean
It is always greater than the mean
quiz.e: Because the Normal distribution is symmetric, mean = median = mode.

quiz.q: Which is the best tool to formally assess Normality using calculator/software output?
quiz.e: The Normal probability plot is specifically designed to assess how well data fit a Normal model.

quiz.q: A Normal distribution has σ = 0. What does this imply?
o: Impossible for real data; SD must be positive
All values equal the mean exactly
quiz.e: An SD of 0 would mean zero variability — every value equal to the mean — which real continuous Normal data cannot have (σ > 0 by definition of the model).

quiz.q: Which pair of z-scores captures the middle 95% of a standard Normal distribution most precisely?
quiz.e: The precise z-value for 95% (2.5% in each tail) is ±1.96, though ±2 is the Empirical Rule approximation.

quiz.q: A company's part diameters are N(2.00, 0.01) cm. What proportion of parts are between 1.98 and 2.02 cm?
quiz.e: 1.98 and 2.02 are μ ± 2σ, capturing about 95% by the Empirical Rule.

quiz.q: A scatterplot shows points closely following an upward line. This suggests:
quiz.e: Points trending upward tightly indicate a strong positive linear correlation.

quiz.q: Correlation r = -0.92 indicates:
quiz.e: r close to -1 indicates a strong negative linear relationship.

quiz.q: Which value of r indicates the weakest linear relationship?
quiz.e: r close to 0 indicates little to no linear relationship.

quiz.q: If the regression line is ŷ = 5 + 2x, the slope means:
o: y increases by 5 for each unit increase in x
y increases by 2 for each unit increase in x
x increases by 2 for each unit increase in y
The line passes through the origin
quiz.e: The slope (2) represents the predicted change in y per one-unit increase in x.

quiz.q: Given b = 3, sx = 2, sy = 6, find r.
If r = 0.8, what is r² and its interpretation?
o: 0.64; 64% of variation in y explained by x
0.8; 80% of variation in y explained by x
quiz.e: r² = 0.8² = 0.64, meaning 64% of the variation in y is explained by the linear relationship with x.

quiz.q: A residual is calculated as:
quiz.e: Residual = observed y minus predicted ŷ.

quiz.q: A residual plot shows a clear curved (U-shaped) pattern. This suggests:
o: The linear model is NOT appropriate; relationship may be nonlinear
quiz.e: A curved residual pattern indicates the data have a nonlinear relationship not captured by the line.

quiz.q: An influential point in regression is one that:
o: Substantially changes the regression line if removed
Is always the point with the largest y-value
quiz.e: Influential points, often with extreme x-values, significantly alter the slope/intercept when removed.

quiz.q: The sum of the residuals for a least-squares regression line is always:
quiz.e: By the least-squares property, positive and negative residuals cancel exactly to zero.

quiz.q: Which of these does correlation NOT measure?
quiz.e: Correlation measures association, never causation.

quiz.q: A least-squares regression line always passes through:
quiz.e: The LSRL always passes through the point of means (x̄, ȳ).

quiz.q: If x and y have correlation r = 0.6, then y and x (switching axes) have correlation:
quiz.e: Correlation is symmetric — it does not depend on which variable is called x or y.

quiz.q: Extrapolation refers to:
o: Predicting y for x-values within the observed range
Predicting y for x-values far outside the observed range
quiz.e: Extrapolation is predicting outside the range of observed x-values, which is unreliable.

quiz.q: A study finds ice cream sales and drowning deaths are positively correlated. The best explanation is:
o: A lurking variable (hot weather) causes both to increase
The correlation is definitely due to chance
quiz.e: Both variables increase in summer due to a lurking (confounding) variable: warm weather.

quiz.q: Which transformation is commonly used to linearize exponential growth data before regression?
o: Taking the square root of x
quiz.e: For exponential relationships, plotting log(y) vs. x often linearizes the data.

quiz.q: A scatterplot's form is described as 'curved.' Which statistic is inappropriate to summarize this relationship?
quiz.e: Correlation r only quantifies linear association, so it's a poor summary for a clearly curved pattern.

quiz.q: If the standard deviation of residuals (s) is small, this suggests:
o: Poor predictions using the regression line
Good predictions; points are close to the line
The line has a negative slope
quiz.e: A small s means the observed values are, on average, close to their predicted values.

quiz.q: Given x̄ = 10, ȳ = 50, and slope b = 4, find the y-intercept a.
Using ŷ = 10 + 4x, predict y when x = 5.
Which best describes 'strength' in a scatterplot?
o: How closely points follow the pattern/form
Whether the slope is positive or negative
quiz.e: Strength refers to how tightly the points cluster around the trend (form).

quiz.q: A negative residual means:
o: The observed value is above the regression line
The observed value is below the regression line
quiz.e: A negative residual (y − ŷ < 0) means the actual value fell below the predicted value.

quiz.q: If r = 0, this means:
o: No relationship of any kind exists
No LINEAR relationship exists (there could still be a strong nonlinear one)
quiz.e: r=0 rules out linear association but does not rule out other (e.g., curved) relationships.

quiz.q: Which point would most likely be influential in a regression?
o: A point near x̄ with a small residual
A point with an extreme x-value far from the rest
A point exactly on the regression line
quiz.e: Points with extreme (high-leverage) x-values have the most potential to influence the slope.

quiz.q: What does the coefficient of determination NOT tell you?
o: The proportion of variation in y explained by x
Whether the relationship is linear (must check residual plot too)
How well the model fits compared to using ȳ alone
quiz.e: r² alone doesn't confirm linearity — you must examine the residual plot to check the linear model is appropriate.

quiz.q: Correlation is unitless because:
o: It is calculated using standardized (z-score) values
quiz.e: r is computed from the average product of standardized x and y values, removing units.

quiz.q: A regression's residual plot shows random scatter around zero with no pattern. This means:
o: The linear model is a poor fit
The linear model is a reasonable fit
quiz.e: Random, patternless residuals support that a linear model is appropriate for the data.

quiz.q: Which is true if two variables have a strong positive association but r is calculated as low (e.g., 0.1)?
o: The data must be normally distributed
quiz.e: A visually strong but non-linear association can still yield a low r, since r measures only linear strength.

quiz.q: Which measure describes the typical prediction error of a regression in the units of y?
quiz.e: s, the standard deviation of the residuals, estimates the typical size of prediction errors.

quiz.q: A scatterplot of weight (x) vs. height (y) shows a moderate positive linear trend with r=0.65. What is r²?
Doubling every x-value in a data set (with y unchanged) affects r how?
quiz.e: Correlation is invariant to linear transformations (scaling/shifting) of either variable.

quiz.q: A 'lurking variable' is:
o: A variable not measured that influences both the explanatory and response variables
Always the cause of the outcome
quiz.e: A lurking variable is unmeasured but affects the apparent relationship between the two studied variables.

quiz.q: Which of the following would make extrapolation especially risky?
o: Predicting for an x-value within the data range
Predicting for an x-value slightly outside the data range where the trend clearly continues
Predicting for an x-value far outside the observed range, where the relationship may change
Using the regression equation as given
quiz.e: Far outside the observed range, there's no evidence the same linear trend continues, making predictions unreliable.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of a residual plot?
o: To assess whether a linear model is appropriate for the data
To find outliers in x only
quiz.e: Residual plots reveal patterns (curvature, changing spread) that indicate whether linear regression is suitable.

quiz.q: A regression of study hours (x) on test score (y) gives ŷ = 60 + 3x. Predict the score for 10 hours studied.
In the equation ŷ = 60 + 3x for study hours and test scores, the intercept 60 means:
o: The predicted score with 0 hours studied
quiz.e: The y-intercept is the predicted y-value when x = 0, here 0 hours of studying.

quiz.q: Which correlation value would produce the steepest positive regression slope, all else equal?
quiz.e: With sx and sy fixed, a larger positive r produces a steeper positive slope since b = r(sy/sx).

quiz.q: A scatterplot shows no visible pattern between x and y at all. The correlation r is likely:
quiz.e: No visible association suggests weak or no linear relationship, so r should be near 0.

quiz.q: Which is true about r² compared to r?
o: r² and r are always equal
r² has the same sign as the slope
quiz.e: Since r² is a squared value, it always falls between 0 and 1 (0% to 100%).

quiz.q: A residual plot shows increasing spread of points as x increases (a 'fan' shape). This indicates:
quiz.e: A fan-shaped residual plot shows that variability in y is not constant across x, violating a key regression assumption.

quiz.q: A pollster selects every 10th name from an alphabetical list after a random start. This is a:
quiz.e: Selecting every kth individual after a random start defines a systematic sample.

quiz.q: A researcher divides a school into homogeneous groups by grade level and takes an SRS from each. This is:
quiz.e: Dividing into similar (homogeneous) strata and sampling within each is stratified sampling.

quiz.q: A researcher randomly selects 5 entire classrooms out of 40 and surveys every student in those classrooms. This is:
quiz.e: Randomly selecting whole (heterogeneous) groups/clusters and sampling everyone within them is cluster sampling.

quiz.q: A magazine asks readers to call in and vote on an issue. This method suffers from:
quiz.e: Only motivated individuals choose to respond, which is voluntary response bias.

quiz.q: A survey has a low response rate, and the people who did respond feel very differently from typical people. This is:
quiz.e: When responders differ systematically from non-responders due to low response rate, this is nonresponse bias.

quiz.q: Which best allows researchers to conclude cause-and-effect?
o: Random assignment in a controlled experiment
quiz.e: Random assignment in a well-designed experiment is the key tool for establishing causation.

quiz.q: A study observes that people who exercise regularly have lower rates of heart disease, without assigning exercise. This is a(n):
quiz.e: No treatment is imposed — researchers just observe and measure existing behavior, making it observational.

quiz.q: Which is a potential confounding variable in an observational study linking coffee drinking to heart disease?
o: The type of coffee cup used
Smoking, if smokers also tend to drink more coffee
quiz.e: Smoking could independently affect heart disease and also correlate with coffee drinking, confounding the relationship.

quiz.q: The three key principles of a well-designed experiment are:
quiz.e: Control, randomize, and replicate are the three core principles of experimental design.

quiz.q: A placebo is used in an experiment to:
o: Control for the placebo effect (response to any treatment)
Eliminate the need for a control group
quiz.e: A placebo lets researchers separate the treatment's real effect from psychological response to receiving any treatment.

quiz.q: In a double-blind experiment:
o: Only subjects don't know their treatment
Only researchers don't know the treatments
Neither subjects nor those assessing outcomes know which treatment was given
No one knows the study is happening
quiz.e: Double-blind means both the subjects and the evaluators are unaware of treatment assignment, reducing bias.

quiz.q: Random assignment in an experiment primarily helps to:
o: Guarantee a representative sample of the population
Balance out lurking variables between treatment groups
Eliminate the need for a control group
quiz.e: Randomly assigning subjects balances known and unknown lurking variables across groups on average.

quiz.q: Which allows results to be generalized to a larger population?
quiz.e: Random sampling from a population is what permits generalizing sample results back to that population.

quiz.q: A study uses random sampling but not random assignment. What can it conclude?
o: Cause and effect for the population
Association only, generalizable to the population
Cause and effect, but only for the sample
quiz.e: Random sampling allows generalization, but without random assignment causation cannot be established — only association.

quiz.q: A study uses random assignment but the subjects were a convenience sample (not randomly selected). What can it conclude?
o: Causation, but only for the subjects studied (not generalizable)
Causation, generalizable to the whole population
quiz.e: Random assignment supports causal conclusions, but without random sampling, results can't be generalized beyond the subjects studied.

quiz.q: Blocking in experimental design is best described as:
o: Grouping similar experimental units before randomly assigning treatments within each group
Assigning all similar subjects to the same treatment
Removing subjects that don't fit a pattern
quiz.e: Blocking groups similar units first, then randomizes treatment within each block to reduce variability.

quiz.q: A matched pairs design is a special case of:
quiz.e: Matched pairs designs use blocks of exactly two units (e.g., twins, or before/after on the same subject).

quiz.q: Which scenario best fits a matched-pairs design?
o: Randomly assigning 100 unrelated subjects to two treatments
Measuring each subject's response under both treatment A and treatment B
Taking an SRS of a population
quiz.e: Testing both treatments on the same subject (or matched subjects) forms natural pairs — a matched-pairs design.

quiz.q: A study on plant growth uses different levels of sunlight and water as separate factors. This describes:
o: A completely randomized design with one factor
quiz.e: Studying two or more factors (sunlight and water) simultaneously is a factorial design.

quiz.q: Undercoverage in a sampling method means:
o: The response rate is too low
Certain groups are systematically excluded from the sampling frame
quiz.e: Undercoverage happens when part of the population has no chance of being selected, e.g., a phone survey missing those without phones.

quiz.q: Which of these best reduces response bias due to sensitive question wording?
o: Using neutral, clearly worded questions and possibly anonymous responses
quiz.e: Neutral wording and anonymity encourage more honest responses, reducing response bias.

quiz.q: A census differs from a sample because a census:
o: Selects a random subset of the population
Attempts to collect data from every individual in the population
quiz.e: A census surveys the entire population, not just a subset.

quiz.q: In a well-designed experiment, replication means:
o: Repeating the entire experiment in another country
Applying each treatment to enough experimental units to reduce chance variation
quiz.e: Replication involves using enough subjects per treatment group so that observed differences aren't due to chance alone.

quiz.q: Which is an experimental unit in a study testing three fertilizers on tomato plants?
quiz.e: The experimental unit is the individual object/subject that receives a treatment — here, each plant.

quiz.q: A lurking variable that affects both the explanatory and response variables, creating a misleading association, is called a:
quiz.e: A confounding variable's effect on the outcome can't be separated from that of the explanatory variable.

quiz.q: Which design would best control for a strong age effect on a health outcome when comparing two treatments?
o: Block by age group, then randomize treatment within each block
quiz.e: Blocking by age removes age as a source of variability, letting researchers isolate the treatment effect more clearly.

quiz.q: Which of the following is true about observational studies?
o: They can never provide useful information
They can suggest associations that experiments might later test causally
quiz.e: Observational studies are valuable for identifying associations for further experimental investigation, but not causation on their own.

quiz.q: Random sampling error refers to:
o: Bias from a poor sampling method
The natural variability between samples from the same population, expected even with proper random sampling
quiz.e: Sampling error is unavoidable natural variation among different random samples, not a mistake or bias.

quiz.q: A poorly worded survey question that suggests a 'correct' answer creates:
quiz.e: Leading question wording is a classic cause of response bias.

quiz.q: Which best distinguishes a completely randomized design from a randomized block design?
o: CRD ignores any blocking variable; RBD groups similar units before randomizing
CRD is always larger than RBD
CRD is only for observational studies
quiz.e: A completely randomized design assigns treatments to all units at random with no blocking, unlike a randomized block design.

quiz.q: Which best describes 'control' as an experimental design principle?
o: Controlling all subjects to receive the same treatment
Comparing treatment(s) against a baseline (like a control or placebo group) to isolate the treatment's effect
Selecting subjects randomly from the population
quiz.e: Control means comparing outcomes against a baseline group to attribute differences specifically to the treatment.

quiz.q: A study assigns treatments to whichever subjects volunteer for them first. This design has a problem because:
o: Lack of random assignment allows confounding between subject characteristics and treatment
quiz.e: Without random assignment, subject characteristics can be linked to treatment choice, confounding the results.

quiz.q: Which two features together allow both causal AND generalizable conclusions?
o: Large sample size and long study duration
quiz.e: Random sampling permits generalization; random assignment permits causal claims — together, both types of conclusions are supported.

quiz.q: In a clinical drug trial, which group receives no active treatment for comparison purposes?
quiz.e: The control (often placebo) group serves as the baseline for comparison against the treatment group.

quiz.q: A study is retrospective if it:
o: Looks back at existing records or historical data to find associations
Randomly assigns subjects to treatments going forward
Follows the same subjects forward in time
quiz.e: Retrospective (case-control) studies look backward at existing data, unlike prospective (cohort) studies that follow subjects forward.

quiz.q: Why can't undercoverage be fixed simply by increasing the sample size?
o: Because it is a bias problem, not a sample-size problem, so excluded groups remain excluded regardless of n
Because larger samples always cost more
Because larger samples always increase bias
Because it is impossible to have undercoverage with SRS
quiz.e: Bias is a systematic error in method, not something averaged away by more observations of the same flawed process.

quiz.q: A survey of a school's students obtained by asking only students in the cafeteria at lunchtime is an example of:
quiz.e: Selecting whoever is conveniently available (students in the cafeteria) is a convenience sample, prone to bias.

quiz.q: Which of the following would most improve a poorly designed observational study?
o: Identifying and measuring potential confounding variables
quiz.e: Measuring potential confounders lets researchers statistically account for them, even though causation still cannot be proven.

quiz.q: A weight-loss study assigns the first 20 volunteers to Diet A and the next 20 to Diet B (not randomly). This design flaw is called:
o: Lack of random assignment, risking confounding (e.g., time-related factors)
quiz.e: Non-random assignment by arrival order can introduce confounding, since early vs. late volunteers might differ systematically.

quiz.q: Which of the following best describes 'generalizability' of a study's conclusions?
o: Whether the conclusion applies only to the exact subjects studied or to a broader population
Whether the study used a placebo
quiz.e: Generalizability concerns how broadly results can be extended, which depends on random sampling from the population of interest.

quiz.q: If P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.4 and A, B are mutually exclusive, find P(A or B).
quiz.e: Mutually exclusive events: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) = 0.3+0.4 = 0.7.

quiz.q: If P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4, P(A and B) = 0.2, find P(A or B).
If P(A) = 0.6, find P(not A).
quiz.e: Complement rule: P(not A) = 1 - 0.6 = 0.4.

quiz.q: Two events A and B are mutually exclusive with P(A) > 0 and P(B) > 0. Are they independent?
quiz.e: If both have positive probability, mutually exclusive events cannot be independent since P(A and B)=0 ≠ P(A)P(B).

quiz.q: If P(A) = 0.3, P(B) = 0.5, and A and B are independent, find P(A and B).
quiz.e: Independent events: P(A and B) = P(A)×P(B) = 0.3×0.5 = 0.15.

quiz.q: Using a two-way table, P(A|B) is calculated as:
quiz.e: By definition, P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B).

quiz.q: A bag has 5 red and 3 blue marbles. Two are drawn without replacement. Are the draws independent?
o: No, probabilities change after each draw
quiz.e: Removing a marble changes the composition of the bag, so the probability of the second draw depends on the first (dependent events).

quiz.q: A die is rolled twice (with replacement). P(first roll is 6 and second roll is 6) equals:
quiz.e: Independent rolls: P = (1/6)×(1/6) = 1/36.

quiz.q: A jar has 4 red and 6 green candies. One is drawn, not replaced, then a second is drawn. Find P(both red).
quiz.e: Without replacement: P(1st red)=4/10, then P(2nd red|1st red)=3/9, so P = 4/10 × 3/9.

quiz.q: What does the Law of Large Numbers state?
o: As the number of trials increases, the observed relative frequency approaches the true probability
Probabilities always equal 0.5 in large samples
quiz.e: The Law of Large Numbers describes convergence of observed frequency to the theoretical probability with more trials.

quiz.q: In a simulation, more trials generally lead to:
o: More accurate estimates of the true probability
quiz.e: By the Law of Large Numbers, increasing trials improves the accuracy of a simulation's estimate.

quiz.q: Which is the correct order of steps in designing a simulation?
o: Run trials, then state assumptions, then assign digits
State assumptions, assign digits/outcomes, run many trials, compute results
Assign digits, then compute results, then state assumptions
quiz.e: The proper simulation process starts with stating assumptions, then assigning digits/outcomes, running trials, then analyzing results.

quiz.q: 'At least one' probability problems are usually easiest solved using:
quiz.e: Computing P(none) and subtracting from 1 is typically much simpler than directly computing 'at least one.'

quiz.q: A basketball player makes 70% of free throws. Find the probability of making at least one of two independent shots.
A two-way table shows 40 males, 60 females; 30 males and 45 females own a car. Find P(owns a car | male).
quiz.e: Conditional probability restricts to the male row: 30 car owners out of 40 males = 30/40 = 0.75.

quiz.q: In the same table (40 males, 60 females; 30 male car owners, 45 female car owners), is car ownership independent of gender?
o: Yes, because sample size is large
quiz.e: Since P(car|male) = P(car|female) = 0.75, matching the overall marginal probability, ownership is independent of gender here.

quiz.q: A tree diagram is most useful for:
o: Finding the mean of a data set
Organizing sequential/conditional probabilities and multiplying along branches
quiz.e: Tree diagrams visually break down multi-stage random processes, letting you multiply probabilities along each path.

quiz.q: If P(A and B) = 0, then A and B must be:
quiz.e: A probability of 0 for both occurring together defines mutually exclusive (disjoint) events.

quiz.q: A weather forecaster says there's a 30% chance of rain today and 30% chance tomorrow, assumed independent. Find P(rain both days).
quiz.e: Independent events multiply: 0.3 × 0.3 = 0.09.

quiz.q: For events A and B, P(A) = 0.4, P(B|A) = 0.5. Find P(A and B).
quiz.e: General multiplication rule: P(A and B) = P(A)×P(B|A) = 0.4×0.5 = 0.2.

quiz.q: A standard deck has 52 cards. What is P(drawing a heart)?
quiz.e: There are 13 hearts out of 52 cards: 13/52 = 1/4.

quiz.q: Rolling two dice, what is P(sum equals 7)?
quiz.e: There are 6 combinations that sum to 7 out of 36 total outcomes: 6/36 = 1/6.

quiz.q: A random digit table assigns digits 0-6 to 'success' and 7-9 to 'failure' to simulate a probability of:
quiz.e: Digits 0-6 cover 7 out of 10 digits, so 'success' probability = 0.7.

quiz.q: Which best describes 'independent trials' in a simulation of coin flips?
o: Each flip's outcome affects the next flip
Each flip has no effect on the probability of the next flip
Flips must alternate heads and tails
quiz.e: Independent trials mean prior outcomes don't change the probability of future outcomes, as with fair coin flips.

quiz.q: Given P(A) = 0.2 and P(B) = 0.3, and A, B are independent, find P(A or B).
Which statement about conditional probability is TRUE?
o: P(A|B) restricts the sample space to only outcomes where B occurred
Conditional probability cannot be computed from two-way tables
quiz.e: Conditioning on B narrows focus to only the B outcomes, from which we then find the proportion that are also A.

quiz.q: A spinner has 4 equal sections: red, blue, green, yellow. Spun twice, find P(both spins are red).
quiz.e: Independent spins: (1/4)×(1/4) = 1/16.

quiz.q: Which situation involves sampling WITH replacement (independent draws)?
o: Drawing cards from a deck without putting them back
Rolling the same die multiple times
Selecting people for a survey without replacement
Dealing cards in a card game
quiz.e: Rolling a die repeatedly doesn't change the die's properties between rolls, keeping the trials independent.

quiz.q: A quality control check finds 5% of items defective. Two items are checked independently. Find P(neither is defective).
quiz.e: P(neither defective) = 0.95 × 0.95 = 0.9025.

quiz.q: Which formula represents the general addition rule for any two events?
quiz.e: The general addition rule subtracts the overlap to avoid double-counting: P(A or B) = P(A)+P(B)−P(A and B).

quiz.q: Two events with P(A) = 0.5 and P(A and B) = 0.5 imply which relationship?
o: A and B are mutually exclusive
B must contain A entirely (A is a subset of B, in probability terms P(A|B) relates as such)
A and B cannot both occur
quiz.e: Since P(A and B) equals P(A) fully, event A always occurs whenever considering the intersection, indicating A is essentially contained within the scenario of B occurring together with A fully.

quiz.q: A jar has 3 red and 2 blue balls; two balls are drawn without replacement. Find P(2nd is blue | 1st is red).
quiz.e: After removing a red ball, 2 blue remain out of 4 total balls: 2/4.

quiz.q: If A and B are independent events with P(A) = 0.6 and P(A and B) = 0.24, find P(B).
quiz.e: Independent events: P(A and B) = P(A)P(B) → 0.24 = 0.6×P(B) → P(B) = 0.4.

quiz.q: A survey shows P(likes math) = 0.5, P(likes science) = 0.6, P(likes both) = 0.3. Find P(likes math or science).
Using the same survey data, are 'likes math' and 'likes science' independent?
o: No, since 0.5×0.6=0.3 does not equal something else
quiz.e: Since P(math)×P(science) = 0.5×0.6 = 0.3 = P(both), these events are independent in this scenario.

quiz.q: Which of these correctly uses a tree diagram's branches?
o: Add along one path, multiply across separate paths
Multiply along one path, add across separate paths
Multiply along one path, subtract across separate paths
Add along one path, add across separate paths
quiz.e: Multiply probabilities along a single branch path; add probabilities across different paths leading to the same outcome.

quiz.q: A machine produces defective items 2% of the time, independently. Find the probability the first defective item occurs on the 3rd item produced (first two are fine).
quiz.e: P(non-defective, non-defective, defective) = 0.98 × 0.98 × 0.02 (this is also the geometric distribution setup).

quiz.q: Which best explains why 'independent' and 'mutually exclusive' are often confused?
o: They are actually the same concept
Both involve two events, but independence concerns whether probabilities change, while mutual exclusivity concerns whether both can occur at all
Mutually exclusive events always have equal probabilities
quiz.e: Though both describe relationships between two events, they capture fundamentally different ideas: influence on probability vs. simultaneous occurrence.

quiz.q: A spinner with regions A (40%), B (35%), C (25%) is spun once. Find P(not A).
A coin is flipped 3 times. Find P(at least one head).
quiz.e: P(at least one head) = 1 − P(all tails) = 1 − (1/2)³ = 1 − 1/8 = 7/8.

quiz.q: A discrete random variable X has P(X=0)=0.1, P(X=1)=0.3, P(X=2)=0.4, and P(X=3)=k. What must k equal for this to be a valid probability distribution?
quiz.e: Probabilities must sum to 1: 0.1+0.3+0.4+k=1, so k=0.2.

quiz.q: Using the distribution P(X=0)=0.1, P(X=1)=0.3, P(X=2)=0.4, P(X=3)=0.2, find E(X).
For the distribution P(X=0)=0.1, P(X=1)=0.3, P(X=2)=0.4, P(X=3)=0.2 (μ=1.7), find Var(X).
A random variable X has μ=10 and σ=4. If Y = 5 + 2X, what is μY?
A random variable X has μ=10 and σ=4. If Y = 5 + 2X, what is σY?
quiz.e: SD(a+bX)=|b|·SD(X)=2(4)=8; note the constant 5 does not affect spread.

quiz.q: X has mean 50 and variance 9. If W = 3X − 4, what is Var(W)?
quiz.e: Var(a+bX)=b²Var(X)=3²(9)=81.

quiz.q: Two independent random variables have μX=20, σX=3 and μY=15, σY=4. Find μ(X+Y).
quiz.e: μ(X+Y)=μX+μY=20+15=35, true regardless of independence.

quiz.q: Two independent random variables have σX=3 and σY=4. Find σ(X+Y).
quiz.e: Var(X+Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y)=9+16=25, so σ(X+Y)=√25=5. SDs do not add directly (3+4=7 is wrong).

quiz.q: Two independent random variables have σX=6 and σY=8. Find σ(X−Y).
quiz.e: Var(X−Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y)=36+64=100 (variances always ADD for independent RVs, even for a difference), so σ=√100=10.

quiz.q: A company's daily profit is the sum of two independent divisions' profits: Division A has μ=$2000, σ=$300; Division B has μ=$1500, σ=$400. What is the standard deviation of total daily profit?
Which of these is NOT a requirement for a binomial setting?
o: A fixed number of trials n
Exactly two outcomes per trial with constant probability of success
The probability of success must be at least 0.5
quiz.e: BINS conditions never require p ≥ 0.5 — p can be any value between 0 and 1.

quiz.q: A basketball player makes 30% of her free throws. If she shoots 8 independent free throws, find P(exactly 3 makes).
X is binomial with n=20 and p=0.25. Find μX and σX.
A quality control inspector checks 15 items from a large shipment where 4% are defective. She samples without replacement. Can this be modeled as approximately binomial?
o: No, sampling without replacement is never binomial
Yes, since 15 is less than 10% of a large shipment, dependence is negligible
No, because p is too small
Yes, but only if she replaces each item after checking
quiz.e: The 10% condition says sampling without replacement is approximately independent (binomial-like) when the sample is less than 10% of the population.

quiz.q: For a binomial distribution with n=12 and p=0.5, is the Normal approximation (Large Counts condition) appropriate?
o: No, since n is too small overall
No, since p must equal exactly 0.5 for Normal approximation
quiz.e: Large Counts condition: np=6≥10 and n(1−p)=6≥10, so the Normal approximation is reasonable.

quiz.q: Which scenario describes a geometric random variable rather than a binomial one?
o: Counting the number of heads in 10 coin flips
Counting the number of defective items in a fixed sample of 50
Counting the number of times you roll a die until you get a 6
Counting the number of correct answers on a 20-question quiz
quiz.e: Geometric variables count trials until the FIRST success with no fixed number of trials; the other options have a fixed n.

quiz.q: You roll a fair die repeatedly until you get a 6. Find the probability that the first 6 occurs on the 3rd roll.
A geometric random variable has p=0.2. Find its mean and standard deviation.
If the probability of a component failing a test is 0.1, find the probability that the first failure occurs AFTER the 3rd trial (i.e., the first 3 trials all succeed).
For a binomial random variable, which pair of formulas is correct?
